moments.selftext: We’re sharing a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, one of the deepest problems at the frontier of mathematics. The proof was produced by a group of agents, using an OpenAI next-generation model significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra. The problem concerns whether the description of smooth three-dimensional fluid motion modeled by the Navier-Stokes equations can break down. It has remained unresolved for roughly 90 years.

moments.selftext: I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work. Seb--and everyone else--acted with integrity and generosity throughout. Initially we believed the other team had also solved the problem. We wanted to collaborate and do a joint release. When we learned that they had Euler but not Navier-Stokes, we offered to let them go first, to suggest that they should be the ones to get the prize, and optionally for Tristan to be the lead author on a rewrite of the OpenAI proof. We felt it was challenging to offer the same to Levent (an Anthropic employee), who was not willing to talk or coordinate with us anyway. We were open to other solutions. We would have greatly preferred coordination. We did not rush to publish even though the other team wasn't communicating with us. The team threatened us with unfounded accusations of plagarism. Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different. It is also worth noting that our latest model can solve many, many other math problems. It is true that we tried this because there were rumors on the internet last week that Anthropic's models had solved a millennium problem and we were curious if ours could do it too.

moments.selftext: Holy cow, its official! OpenAI says its AI has solved the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, a mathematical question unresolved for roughly 90 years. An internal model, described as significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra, powered a group of around 10,000 concurrent agents (see the graph below! Its crazy more powerful than Astra) The agents reached the solution after just 88 hours. Lean formalization and verification took another 17 hours via GPT-6 Astra. The reported result: smooth three-dimensional fluid motion can develop a singularity in finite time under a smooth external force, while total energy remains finite. OpenAI is sharing the proof and its Lean formalization. 130 billion output tokens went into the Navier–Stokes effort alone. The internal model is still training. Welcome to the singularity!

moments.selftext: THIS IS HISTORY I don't know if you realize what this means. My hands are shaking... Are we seeing the first sign of emerging ASI (artificial superintelligence)? The first glimpses of an artificial intelligence beyond that of any human. Navier–Stokes, no less... SOLVED BY AI! If confirmed, this is a historic milestone. It would be the second Millennium Prize Problem to be solved. The first was the Poincaré conjecture, solved by Grigori Perelman in his 2003 papers. The implications of this make me think we’re past the point of just asking whether we’re on the verge of AGI (we possibly already are), and that we could be about to collide head-on with an exponential explosion of intelligence. The singularity... Straight to ASI! According to OpenAI, around 10,000 coordinated AI agents arrived at the solution in about 88 hours, plus another 17 for formalization and verification in Lean. This is insane. Just 100 hours to find a solution to a problem that had remained unsolved for around 90 years! What's next? HOLY SHIT.

moments.title: I love that the only monumental bronze equestrian statue from ancient Rome to survive is one of Marcus Aurelius—a man who had little concern for being remembered forever. The statue of Marcus Aurelius was likely created
moments.selftext: I love that the only monumental bronze equestrian statue from ancient Rome to survive is one of Marcus Aurelius—a man who had little concern for being remembered forever. The statue of Marcus Aurelius was likely created around 176 CE, following his military campaigns against Germanic tribes. Ancient Rome was once home to numerous monumental equestrian statues. Late Roman accounts mention 22 of these massive “great horses,” yet the statue of Marcus Aurelius is the only one that has survived intact. Its preservation was largely due to a historical misunderstanding. During the Middle Ages, people mistakenly believed the statue portrayed Constantine, the first Roman emperor to embrace Christianity. Because of this mistaken identity, it was spared while countless other ancient bronze statues were melted down and their valuable metal repurposed. That makes the statue’s survival particularly ironic. In Meditations, Marcus Aurelius often wrote about how fleeting fame, reputation, and human memory truly are. He believed that, with enough time, both those who are remembered and those who remember them will eventually disappear.
